clue.text: Means of preserving secret loves in disguise ?

indicators.note: something in disguise has its appearance changed, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: love is zero in tennis scoring, the letter O, so two loves give two Os

explanation.surface: Someone hides their secret love affairs behind a disguise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in disguise' shuffles SECRET with OO (two loves) into the wood preservative.
explanation.definitionFit: This tar-oil liquid is painted on fences and timber to protect the wood from rot.

clue.text: Pusillanimous playwright

explanation.definitionFit: Lacking courage, a craven person; also Noel ____, the English dramatist of Private Lives.

clue.text: Worthy, competent successor to this paper, possibly

indicators.note: a successor comes after, so the word for competent follows the rearranged paper
possibly says the paper's name might be rearranged

parts.note: the clue appeared in The Times
competent means able

explanation.surface: A capable heir to this newspaper would be a worthy figure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'this paper' is The Times, where the clue appeared; 'possibly' rearranges its name, and 'successor to' sets the word for competent after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Deserving respect or high regard.

clue.text: Kipling's dog, obedient if civil

explanation.surface: Kipling's dog is obedient as long as it is polite.
explanation.walkthrough: 'obedient' and 'civil' each precede the word: 'your obedient ...' signs off a letter, and a civil ... works for the state.
explanation.definitionFit: Kipling wrote 'Thy ____ a Dog', told by a dog; letters end 'your obedient ____', and a government official is a civil one.

clue.text: Angler's catch is lifted right out

indicators.note: in a down clue lifting something reads it from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A fisherman's catch is hauled clean out of the water.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'is lifted' reads the abbreviation upwards; 'right out' looks like 'completely out' but is two pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: A freshwater game fish prized by those who fish with a rod.

clue.text: Men from the East bring one article in a ship

indicators.note: the first pieces are placed inside the letters for a ship, so they sit within it

parts.note: SS is the abbreviation for steamship
the Roman numeral for one is I
an is the indefinite article

explanation.surface: Eastern men bring something aboard a vessel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Men from the East' reads as the Magi, but it simply means people of Asia; 'in' sets one and the article inside A plus the ship abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Asia, the continent to the east of Europe, are Asians.

clue.text: Smart sort of coat

explanation.definitionFit: Stylish and fashionable in British slang; also a loose, flared lady's coat style of the 1930s.

clue.text: Duke of Milan's servant makes one earl

indicators.note: makes says these letters are made into a new word

parts.note: the Roman numeral for one is I

explanation.surface: A duke's servant is elevated to an earl.
explanation.walkthrough: Prospero, the rightful Duke of Milan in Shakespeare's The Tempest, is served by the airy spirit; 'makes' rearranges I + EARL.
explanation.definitionFit: The spirit who serves Prospero in The Tempest.

clue.text: Application for one racing tip is held by the sergeant-major

indicators.note: held by means the pieces are contained within the abbreviation

parts.note: SM is the abbreviation for sergeant-major
the Roman numeral for one is I
a nap is a tipster's best bet of the day in horse racing
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sergeant-major keeps a racing tip for himself.
explanation.walkthrough: In racing, a tipster's nap is the day's most confident selection. 'Application' looks like a form to fill in but means a medical poultice.
explanation.definitionFit: A mustard plaster, a poultice applied to the skin as a remedy.

clue.text: Like Jorrocks's best mount, we hear, it gives no flaming trouble

indicators.note: we hear says the words are judged by how they sound when spoken

parts.note: as (like) + best + 'oss, the hunting grocer Jorrocks's h-dropping word for horse

explanation.surface: Jorrocks's favourite horse never causes any bother.
explanation.walkthrough: John Jorrocks, Surtees's Cockney hunting grocer, drops his aitches, so his best horse is his 'best 'oss'; 'Like' gives AS.
explanation.definitionFit: A fibrous mineral used for fireproofing because it will not burn.

clue.text: The end of the line for Corporal Violet?

definitions.text: The end of the line for Corporal Violet?

parts.words: The end of the line for Corporal Violet?
parts.note: a London railway terminus shares its name with the 1815 battle that ended Napoleon's career; 'Corporal Violet' was a Bonapartist nickname for him

explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon was the 'Little Corporal', and his supporters used the violet as a secret emblem. The London terminus is literally the end of a railway line, and the battle it is named after was the end of the line for him.
explanation.definitionFit: A terminus where trains finish their run, named after Napoleon's final defeat in Belgium.

clue.text: Like lions up in arms

parts.note: in heraldry (coats of arms) a lion rearing on its hind legs has a special term, which also means wild and unchecked

explanation.walkthrough: 'up in arms' looks like 'angry', but 'arms' is heraldry, where a lion standing up on its hind legs is described this way.
explanation.definitionFit: The heraldic term for a beast reared up on its hind legs, also used for unrestrained growth.

clue.text: Shrove Tuesday drink ?

parts.note: Shrove Tuesday is pancake day, when pancakes are tossed in the pan; a drink of beaten egg and milk has a name that sounds like tossing an egg

explanation.walkthrough: On Shrove Tuesday (Pancake Day) the British toss pancakes, a batter of egg flipped in the pan, which is also the name of a frothy egg drink.
explanation.definitionFit: A drink of beaten egg with milk or alcohol, the name also describing pancake tossing.

clue.text: Hamper introduction of summer time in court perhaps

indicators.note: the time abbreviation is placed inside the rearranged letters of court
perhaps suggests the letters of court could be arranged another way

parts.note: BST is British Summer Time

explanation.surface: Bringing in summer time might hinder proceedings in a law court.
explanation.walkthrough: 'court perhaps' looks like a lawcourt example, but 'perhaps' rearranges the word, and 'in' sets the summer-time abbreviation inside the result.
explanation.definitionFit: To hinder or get in the way of something is to block its progress.

clue.text: In the minority

parts.note: minority here is the legal state of being a minor, not the smaller group

explanation.walkthrough: 'minority' seems to mean the smaller number, but legally it is the period of being a minor, too young.
explanation.definitionFit: Too young in law to vote, drink or sign contracts.

clue.text: Five handy Christmas gifts for a fine, if horsy, lady

definitions.text: Five handy Christmas gifts for a fine, if horsy, lady

parts.words: Five handy Christmas gifts for a fine, if horsy, lady
parts.note: the carol's true love gives five golden ones on the fifth day, and the nursery rhyme's fine lady on a white horse wears them on her fingers

explanation.walkthrough: Two rhymes: 'The Twelve Days of Christmas' (five gold ones) and 'Ride a cock-horse to Banbury Cross', whose fine lady has them on her fingers; 'handy' because they are worn on the hand.
explanation.definitionFit: Bands of gold worn on the fingers, as in both the carol and the nursery rhyme.

clue.text: Titanic disaster ? The heartless wink

indicators.note: a disaster wrecks things, so the ship's name is broken up
heartless removes the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: After the Titanic disaster, the heartless only wink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'disaster' shuffles TITANIC to NICTITA; 'heartless' removes the H at the centre of THE, leaving TE.
explanation.definitionFit: To blink rapidly, as with the eyelid's third membrane in birds.

clue.text: Dante ante Raphael?

parts.note: ante is Latin for before, so this is a Dante who was pre-Raphael: the poet-painter Dante Gabriel, founder of the Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood

explanation.walkthrough: 'ante Raphael' is Latin for 'before Raphael', i.e. Pre-Raphaelite; the Dante in question is the Victorian painter, not the Florentine poet.
explanation.definitionFit: Dante Gabriel, the Victorian painter and poet who co-founded the Pre-Raphaelites.

clue.text: Love by means of a musical entertainment

parts.note: love is zero in tennis, the letter O
per means by means of, as in per post

explanation.surface: Romance conveyed through a musical show.
explanation.definitionFit: A staged drama set entirely to music, sung by performers with an orchestra.

clue.text: "Queen Mab… drawn… men's noses as they lie asleep" (R & J)

definitions.text: "Queen Mab… drawn… men's noses as they lie asleep" (R & J)

parts.words: "Queen Mab… drawn… men's noses as they lie asleep" (R & J)
parts.note: a fill-in from Mercutio's Queen Mab speech: her chariot is drawn by tiny creatures across sleepers' noses

explanation.walkthrough: In Romeo and Juliet Mercutio says Queen Mab is 'drawn with a team of little atomies' across men's noses; the missing word means across.
explanation.definitionFit: An old word meaning across or from side to side.

clue.text: Send message — kill!

explanation.surface: A terse order to send word and then kill.
explanation.definitionFit: To send off quickly; an official report or newspaper message; to put to death swiftly.

clue.text: Dear old thing !

parts.note: dear here means expensive, so it is a costly old object, not an affectionate greeting

explanation.walkthrough: 'Dear old thing' sounds like a fond greeting, but dear means expensive.
explanation.definitionFit: A valuable collectable from a past era, often costly.

clue.text: Turn back, Sapper Green !

parts.note: a sapper is a soldier of the Royal Engineers, RE
vert is the heraldic word for green

explanation.surface: An order telling a sapper named Green to go back.
explanation.walkthrough: Sappers are army engineers, the Royal Engineers or RE.
explanation.definitionFit: To go back to a former state or habit.

clue.text: Old Bob a lady-killer or an iconoclast?

explanation.surface: Old Bob was either a ladies' man or a breaker of idols.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' marks the first sense as dated slang: a dashing chap like Bob was once a real heartbreaker.
explanation.definitionFit: Dated slang for a strikingly attractive man; also one who breaks things, as an image-breaker destroys religious statues.

clue.text: The prize goes to a protected person

parts.note: a ward is a person under a guardian's protection

explanation.surface: A trophy is presented to someone under protection.
explanation.definitionFit: A trophy or honour given for merit.

clue.text: Heads of state confer on the Equator?

definitions.text: Heads of state confer on the Equator?

parts.words: Heads of state confer on the Equator?
parts.note: leaders talk over a direct emergency phone link, and the Equator is a line where it is very warm

explanation.walkthrough: The Washington-Moscow emergency link is called by this name, and the Equator is literally a warm line round the globe.
explanation.definitionFit: A direct telephone link for urgent contact, famously between Washington and Moscow.

clue.text: There's an hour's difference, north of the lake

indicators.note: difference suggests the letters are made different, rearranged

parts.note: the 's only shows possession or stands for 'is', so it adds no letters: the word before it gives these letters as it is written

explanation.surface: Crossing north of the lake puts you in another time zone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'difference' rearranges the letters of the hour, and the north abbreviation follows; 'an hour's difference' suggests time zones.
explanation.definitionFit: One of North America's five Great Lakes, between Michigan and Ontario.

clue.text: If 1805's old-fashioned, then there you are, Horatio

parts.note: the naval battle of 1805 was fought off Cape Trafalgar
square means conventional or old-fashioned

explanation.surface: Someone tells Horatio that being stuck in 1805 makes him dated.
explanation.walkthrough: Horatio Nelson won the battle of 1805 and stands on his column in this London square, so 'there you are' is where he is.
explanation.definitionFit: The London plaza where Nelson's Column stands, with the admiral on top.

clue.text: Write new edition, leaving out nothing

indicators.note: new tells us the letters of the word are formed afresh in another order
leaving out means a letter is removed from the word edition

parts.note: nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: An author drafts a fresh edition, omitting nothing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaving out' drops O (nothing) from EDITION to leave EDITIN, and 'new' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal, old word for composing or putting into words on paper.

clue.text: Advantage taken by uncle: for instance

explanation.surface: A nephew's uncle takes advantage of him.
explanation.walkthrough: The pawnbroker is called 'uncle' in British slang, and charges this on money lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Benefit or one's own good; also the charge a pawnbroker, nicknamed 'uncle', adds to a loan.
